content.rendered:
April 2026

This issue of Asian Cinema Digest highlights an exciting slate of screenings and programmes — from the Singapore Chinese Film Festival to newly restored video works by Japanese artist Kyoko Michishita, and the rediscovery of Singapore neighbourhoods through film. 

To See

Asian Film Archive: Prasasti / Inscriptions: Unearthing Intertwined Legacies

As part of Asian Film Archive’s contribution to Singapore Biennale, this collaborative programme with Jakarta-based collective Forum Lenteng brings together films that revisit objects, landscapes and archives to question how histories and national narratives are constructed and whose stories are allowed to persist. 

Running till 26 April 2026, don’t miss the chance to catch works from Southeast Asian filmmakers, including Kavich Neang, Lin Htet Aung, Tulapop Saenjaroen, Nguyễn Trinh Thi, and Shireen Seno.

 

14th Singapore Chinese Film Festival 2026

Singapore Chinese Film Festival (SCFF) returns for its 14th edition, bringing a slate of exciting Sinophone releases from 24 April to 3 May 2026.

Explore restored classics such as Patrick Tam’s Love Massacre (1981), starring screen icon Brigette Lin and new releases such as Chong Keat Aun’s Mother Bhumi (2025), where Fan Bingbing delivers a transformative performance as a ritual healer in rural 1990s Malaysia. Don’t miss the Shanghai Film Academy Shorts spotlighting emerging Chinese directors, as well as the documentary showcase, which includes Mary Stephen’s Palimpsest: The Story of a Name (2025).

 

e-flux Film: Kyoko Michishita

For the April 2026 edition of Staff Picks, e-flux Film has collaborated with distribution organisation Vtape to present three films by Japanese artist Kyoko Michishita — Cherry Blossoms (1975), Being Women in Japan Series: Liberation Within My Family (1974), and Video Portraits – Men: Shuntarō Tanikawa (1982). 

One of the first artists in Japan to adopt video technology, Michishita used the medium as an artistic tool to explore feminist principles. Experimental and observational, her films probe the complexities of women’s issues in Japan. Now restored and digitised, this marks the first time in decades that her body of work is available for public viewing.

 

To Attend

Singapore University of Social Sciences: The Rise of China and the Chinese Migrant Woman in Singapore Cinema

Led by film scholar Ng How Wee (senior lecturer at University of Westminster), this talk dissects the cinematic figure of the mainland Chinese migrant woman in Singapore cinema across three decades. Her on-screen meanings are examined through ten feature films, including Yeo Siew Hua’s A Land Imagined (2018) and K. Rajagopal’s A Yellow Bird (2016), responding to the changing political, industrial, and market conditions of Singapore. 

The talk will take place at Singapore University of Social Sciences on 23 April 2026, 7pm, and you can register your interest here.

FFIGS: A Contrary Communing of Cinema

A Contrary Communing of Cinema is a portable film programme and guided walk by independent Singapore collective FFIGS, that takes participants across Chinatown. Moving through the neighbourhood — from Pearl’s Hill Terrace to the rooftop of the Goethe-Institut Singapore — the programme invites participants to experience film alongside the beloved neighbourhood’s landscapes and histories. You can register your interest here.

 

TO LISTEN

Deep Cut: 127. Interview with Kani Releasing: Ariel Esteban Cayer and Pearl Chan

In this episode of Deep Cut, host Wilson travels to Peng Chau Island in Hong Kong to talk to Ariel Esteban Cayer and Pearl Chan, the folks behind Kani Releasing, a North American film distribution company specialising in Asian cinema.

The trio discuss the films in Kani Relasing’s catalogue, such as Marilou Diaz-Abaya’s Moral  (1983) and Patrick Tam’s My Heart Is That Eternal Rose (1989), as well as the motivations behind founding the company and their perspectives on the ever-evolving landscape of theatrical and physical media distribution.

 

Cinema Rex: 063 – The Things You Kill

Filmmakers and hosts of Cinema Rex Podcast Kaveh Mohebbi and Faran Moradi discuss Iranian filmmaker Alireza Khatami’s The Things You Kill (2025), a Turkish-language mystery film following a university professor who gets the help of his gardener to seek vengeance after the sudden death of his mother. Mohebbi and Moradi dissect the film’s exploration of identity and moral ambiguity, while also sharing behind-the-scenes insights and lesser known trivia about the production behind this critically acclaimed film.

 

To Read

The New Yorker: The Unseen Work of One of Iran’s Greatest Filmmakers

For many cinephiles, names like Abbas Kiarostami, Jafar Panahi, and Asghar Farhadi have come to define Iranian cinema. But as Richard Brody, veteran film critic at The New Yorker, suggests, filmmakers like Mani Haghighi deserve equal attention.

Having worked with Kiarostami early in his career, Haghighi has developed a distinct and varied filmography. Brody explores Haghighi’s range, from the black comedy Pig (2018) to the thriller Subtraction (2022), while also reflecting on the challenges of censorship in Iran, and the broader struggle faced by Iranian filmmakers navigating repression and creative constraint.

 

Asian Movie Pulse: Jang Joon-hwan Interview on Save the Green Planet!

Speaking with film critic Panso Kotzathanasis, Korean filmmaker Jang Joon-Hwan revisits his cult classic film Save the Green Planet! (2003). Reflecting on the film’s production and its experimental narrative, Jang considers the conditions of the early 2000s Korean film industry, when such bold, genre-defying works were more readily embraced. The conversation also touches on Yorgos Lanthimos’ 2025 adaptation, Bugonia, and how Jang’s original screenplay has evolved and been adapted for the current age.

 

To Submit

Film Programming Open Call: Rae-Nang

Rae-Nang, a new initiative in Bangkok formed in partnership with Atlas Cinema, London, aims to democratise film exhibition and offer a new model for a community cooperative cinema. Seeking 6 Bangkok-based individuals with an interest in film programming, participants will be led by UK-based curators Cici Peng and Abiba Coulibaly in online sessions and support the development of their programmes.

Participants will present their own screening programmes at the opening of the Rae Nang Cinema on 7 to 9 August 2026, and continue to manage the space alongside the organisers from August 2026 to January 2027. The application guidelines can be found here, and the submission deadline is 1 May 2026.

 

Call for Submissions: SeaShorts Film Festival 2026

Based in Malaysia, SeaShorts Film Festival, screens emerging Southeast Asian short films and is one of the region’s most notable film events. The festival also includes sharing sessions for regional exchange and learning, as well as opportunities for networking and collaboration. The application guidelines can be found here, and the submission deadline is 4 June 2026.

 

Call for Submissions: HKIFF Asian Short Film Fund

The Hong Kong International Film Festival Society (HKIFFS) and NOWNESS Asia, a subsidiary of Meta Media Group, launched the Asian Short Film Fund (ASFF) in 2025 to support emerging Asian filmmakers and promote the development of filmmaking in the region. This second edition returns with three distinguished Asian filmmakers serving as mentors: Lav Diaz, Oh Jung-Wan and Yeh Ju-Feng. The application guidelines can be found here, and the submission deadline is 5 June 2026.

 

Call for Submissions: (blank) Experimental Film Festival

This new film festival, a Southeast Asian collaboration with the BIDEODROMO International Experimental Film and Video Festival, champions experimental works that resist conventional definitions and frameworks of film. Supported by The Substation, selected films will be screened in Singapore and across various venues in Bilbao, Spain. The application guidelines can be found here, and the submission deadline is 1 July 2026.

 

This edition of the Asian Cinema Digest was compiled by Phyllis Chan. The Asian Cinema Digest is a monthly compilation of content taking place internationally involving Asian cinema and the moving image. Featured programmes are not representative of AFA’s views and are unaffiliated to the AFA unless otherwise stated.

March 2026

This issue of the Asian Cinema Digest focuses on women filmmakers across regions and generations. Explore the bold and subversive films of Sari Dalena and Anocha Suwichakornpong, read the perspectives of Clara Law, Arundhati Roy and Bani Khoshnoudi, and discover how women continue to reshape contemporary cinema.

To See

Counter-Archives of a Film Guerrera: A Retrospective of Sari Dalena’s Cinema

Running from March to May, this retrospective of Filipino filmmaker Sari Dalena runs across multiple venues in the Philippines — including the University of the Philippines Film Institute (UP Diliman), Mowelfund Film Institute, University of the Philippines Mindanao, The Green House Cinema (Davao), and Mindanao State University–Iligan Institute of Technology. Curated by Patrick F. Campos, the programme features Dalena’s documentaries, experimental films, and video works as a counter-archive, which foregrounds women’s labour and memory at the margins of official history.

A recipient of the Cultural Center of the Philippines’ Thirteen Artists Award in 2000, the retrospective presents her key works such as Memories of a Forgotten War (2001), The Guerilla Is a Poet (2013) and Cinemartyrs (2025). The retrospective is accompanied by the exhibition Notes Toward a Guerrera Cinema, on view from 28 March to 7 April at the UPFI Ishmael Bernal Gallery.

 

Metrograph at Home: Anocha Suwichakornpong: A Retrospective

Presented on Metrograph’s streaming platform, this retrospective of Thai filmmaker Anocha Suwichakornpong foregrounds her formally inventive approach to grappling with Thailand’s sociopolitical histories. Featuring her landmark feature By the Time It Gets Dark (2016) alongside short films such as Overseas (2012) and The Ambassadors (2018), the programme surveys a filmmaker who persistently challenges cinematic forms while probing the entanglements between memory, history, and lived realities.

 

The 50th Hong Kong International Film Festival

The Hong Kong International Film Festival returns under the theme “50 and Beyond: Framing the Future,” marking a milestone edition that reflects on cinema’s evolving trajectories. Opening on 1 April at the Hong Kong Cultural Centre with We Are All Strangers (2026), the concluding film of Anthony Chen’s Growing-Up Trilogy, the festival brings together an expansive programme spanning regions and decades.

This edition spotlights Chinese auteur Jia Zhangke as its Filmmaker in Focus, featuring works such as Xiao Shan Going Home (1995) and Ash Is the Purest White (2018), which chronicle the social textures of a rapidly modernising China. The festival also presents a special programme, Mary Stephen: Inner Thoughts in Moving Image, dedicated to the Hong Kong-born, Paris-based filmmaker, featuring Ombres de soie (1978), alongside her new feature Palimpsest: The Story of a Name (2025).

 

To Read

Another Gaze: A Conversation with Clara Law

In this conversation with film curator Eleanor Lu, Hong Kong filmmaker Clara Law reflects on her four-decade career shaped by movement across cultures and film industries — from her beginnings at Radio Television Hong Kong to studio filmmaking and, later, independent, self-funded work. Touching on the uncertainty surrounding Hong Kong’s impending handover and the diasporic experiences that recur throughout her films, Law speaks of cinema as a poetic form that weaves together memory and philosophy.

Catch Clara Law’s Farewell China at Oldham Theatre on 4 April 2026, tickets here.

 

Scroll: Arundhati Roy: ‘In Which Annie Gives It Those Ones isn’t a manifesto. It’s just a joyful stance’

“The magic of cinema is that it can preserve a moment and stir it into a cocktail.” — Arundhati Roy

This excerpt from Roy’s new introduction to In Which Annie Gives It Those Ones – The Screenplay revisits the unlikely afterlives of the 1989 television film, written by her and directed by Pradip Krishen. From its circulation on VHS copies to its resurgence online and recent screening at the 2026 Berlinale, Roy reflects on the film’s enduring resonance within India’s shifting political landscape, tracing how its irreverent student politics and countercultural spirit continue to speak to the present.

 

MoMA: Silence Spoken and a Cry in the Dark: Bani Khoshnoudi at the Vanishing Point

Born in Tehran and raised in the United States, filmmaker and artist Bani Khoshnoudi reflects on her return to her birth city in this personal essay, drawing on stills from her film The Vanishing Point (2025). In this reflection, Khoshnoudi moves between personal memory and collective history, as she delves into her feelings of displacement in Tehran. For her, time in the city remains “both circular and repeating, no matter how tragic and dark.

 

To Submit

Call for Project: Docs by the Sea

Docs by the Sea is an international documentary forum in Indonesia dedicated to empowering Asian filmmakers through film labs and pitching forums. Participating filmmakers will get the opportunity to work with highly esteemed international mentors, present their projects, and connect with international industry representatives. The application guidelines can be found here, and the submission deadline is 29 March 2026.

 

Call for Submissions: BIFF Asian Cinema Fund

Busan International Film Festival’s Asian Cinema Fund (ACF) is currently accepting submissions for its Script Development Fund and Asian Network of Documentary Fund. ACF supports projects through the Asian Contents & Film Market, with many receiving critical acclaim at international film festivals. The application guidelines can be found here. The final submission deadline for the Script Development Fund is 13 April 2026, and the Asian Network of Documentary Fund is 20 April 2026.

 

Call for Submissions: 12th Minikino Film Week

Minikino Film Week returns for its 12th edition, taking place from 11 to 18 September 2026 in Bali, Indonesia. The application guidelines can be found here, and the final submission deadline is 27 April 2026. Interested applicants can either submit their works through FilmFreeway or Short Film Depot.

 

Call for Submissions: 2026 KFF International Short Film & XR Competition

Scheduled from 10 to 26 October 2026, the Kaohsiung Film Festival invites submissions for its International Short Film and XR Competition. Open to Asian short films and Extended Reality (XR) works, the festival supports innovative practices that expand the boundaries of cinematic experience. The application guidelines can be found here, and the submission period is from 1 April to 10 June 2026.

 

 

This edition of the Asian Cinema Digest was compiled by Phyllis Chan. The Asian Cinema Digest is a monthly compilation of content taking place internationally involving Asian cinema and the moving image. Featured programmes are not representative of AFA’s views and are unaffiliated to the AFA unless otherwise stated.

content.rendered:
A Secret Portrait of Wan Hoi-Ling (2025) reimagines the life of Wan Hoi-Ling, a pioneering but little-known female director and screenwriter who worked across Hong Kong and Singapore, creating anti-imperialist, anti-colonial films. In this interview, artist Elsa Wong reflects on how she transposed her research into the film’s three-part narrative, working with a variety of materials and techniques, from sourcing found objects to crafting dioramas, experimenting with 16mm film, and developing a multi-language soundtrack. Seeking an alternative to stereotypical portrayals of Wan as a tragic heroine, Elsa offers the viewer an empathetic vision of a woman moving through love, ambition, and loss.

This interview was conducted on August 14, 2025 by AFA film programmer and curator Natalie Khoo and writer Sheryl Gwee. The transcript has been edited for length and clarity.

SHERYL: What drew you to the story of Wan Hoi-Ling, who takes centre stage in your installation?

ELSA: I was really drawn to her story because of how active she was during a very short period of time. Then she disappeared. I read more into it and realised that Wan Hoi-Ling had worked with Hou Yao, as his apprentice. They made many films together and then came to Singapore, where they were stuck because of the Japanese Occupation. It was a very tragic story. The Japanese wanted Hou Yao to make propaganda films, but he refused, so he was executed. Wan Hoi-Ling was imprisoned. 

Years after she was imprisoned, she made two more films, in Singapore. Then she went back to Hong Kong and eventually disappeared. I was intrigued by what she might have been experiencing emotionally, because so much had happened. I began imagining the kind of story I could create around her, as well as the scenarios themselves—the interiors, the landscapes, her perspective, what she might have been feeling. I could picture the details within the frame.

 

SHERYL: Your initial sketches showed a three-channel video installation, which has now evolved into a single-channel projection. Could you tell us more about how you developed the three-part structure of the film?

ELSA: In my research, I noticed three very distinct timelines. The interviews and essays written about Wan Hoi-Ling often went through her filmography to describe both her personal life and her career. They structured it around the films she made during different periods of her life.

So, I began to see it as three parts: first, her time with her partner, when they were making films together. The films from that period were very optimistic and future-oriented.

Then came the second part, when she was alone. The films she made during that time reflected her personal struggles and had a very different tone—more serious and sombre than those she created with her partner.

The third part was when she began to disappear. During this time, she wrote one last script called Love Torn (dir. Kao Li, released 1963), which I thought was a very poetic, all-encompassing title that spoke to her journey across the first two parts.

SHERYL: What about the techniques that you used, such as 16mm film? How did you conceptualise the visuals in relation to the turbulent emotions that she might have been feeling?

ELSA: I went back and forth deciding between portraying the story through live action or through miniatures. I started with a model for the first part, and after making it, I felt a personal touch between me and the object. I don’t personally know Wan Hoi-Ling, but through creating the film, I began to feel a certain closeness to her. So, I decided to use objects to represent different parts of the script.

The film is composed of still-lifes and miniatures, and I chose to shoot it on 16mm. It was quite a challenge because 16mm took much longer, especially with lighting. Most of it had to be a one-take, though I would sometimes shoot a safety. Still, I committed to 16mm because it was a medium used during her time, and I thought it would add to the experience of filming. So much of their work was shot on film, and some of it has been lost—there’s something about the object of the film reel itself that I wanted to bring into this work.

Most of the 16mm was shot on my own, which brought a certain loneliness. When I was arranging the miniatures and moving the cutout of Wan Hoi-Ling around, it was a strange feeling. She wasn’t really present in what I was making, but I felt as though a version of her that I imagined was there. There was a strange sense of both connection and disconnection.

SHERYL: It’s almost as if you’re trying to bridge the gap in time between her story and yours. From what you’ve shared, there’s also a sense of empathy—of you really trying to understand what she was going through.

ELSA: Yeah, that’s a good word, because I don’t think anyone knows what she was truly like as a person, other than that she was very ambitious. I think her ambition, and perhaps her optimism, allowed her to continue after the war. 

 

SHERYL: Could you tell me more about the kinds of motifs that you selected? 

ELSA: One of the first images that kept popping into my mind while planning the scenes was confetti. I kept thinking about the almost euphoric feeling of confetti floating in the air—it creates a climactic sense of joy. But there’s also a point where the confetti falls to the ground, and it evokes a very sad feeling, like the party is over.

The confetti mainly symbolises celebration, a sense of a party, which I wanted to emphasise in the first part. It represents Wan and Hou enjoying their time together—working, creating. Then, when the confetti fades and they sweep it away, it becomes metaphorical, reflecting how that happy, celebratory era has passed.

 

SHERYL: What about the double exposures?

ELSA: I wanted to create a physical overlay of different objects and visuals, symbolically tying them together. The double exposures of confetti, and sometimes of lights, allowed me to experiment with how these elements could seep into another layer of the 16mm film. It was about physically burning these images into the first layer I shot, whether that was a miniature or another object, creating a tactile, layered effect.

SHERYL: What were the other found objects that you used?

ELSA: Besides the miniatures, I also represented Wan and Hou through personal objects, like their shoes. The placement of the objects carried meaning. For example, a pair of shoes sprawled on the floor alongside scripts, indicating that something tragic had happened to Wan and that a part of her had “disappeared” into her work.

Besides using the miniature figures, I wanted to show Wan and Hou together in the frame, physically, using personal objects to evoke presence. For Hou, I included a pair of round glasses similar to the ones in his photos. One particularly difficult scene involved representing his death. I debated between a literal depiction of violence or a more metaphorical approach. Ultimately, I chose to place a pool of blood around his cracked glasses, subtly indicating that violence and death had affected him.

 

SHERYL: I think it’s interesting that you use the shoes, without including a person. There’s a sense of loss and it reflects the act of imagining something that exists only in the gaps, especially since so many of Wan and Hou’s films are not accessible. What do you think you’ve gained through this exploration of the gaps in film history?

ELSA: Because there was a lack of information, I was allowed to be very imaginative. It’s interesting that you point out that there are no people; some scenes have just hands. The scenes with clothing but without people—they’re like ghosts.

When I first watched one of the films AFA shared with me, Spirit of the Overseas Chinese (dir. Wan Hoi-Ling, 1946), I felt a very strange awakening. The language was hard to understand without subtitles because it was in Mandarin, Hokkien, and some other dialects. At the same time, a lot of the landscapes depicted were the Singapore I recognised from photos, but not exactly one I had lived in. I felt a disconnect between myself and those time periods.

I gained a lot by learning about Singapore and Hong Kong, and about how Malay films were pioneering in Singapore in the 1930s. Wan and Hou were invited to make films in Singapore, which was interesting to learn about, along with how the Shaw Brothers initially wanted to make Malay films before moving more into Chinese films.

Prior to this project, I didn’t know of Wan Hoi-Ling’s existence. Reading different essays about her, I realised they all have very limited information. They often describe her in a very sad way, ending with the idea that she couldn’t handle the trauma from the war in Singapore and eventually, the loss of love. It’s almost as if she were a woman who didn’t have her own voice. Whether or not that was true, I decided to write her story in a way that left things with a question mark. She contemplates whether she really is feeling sad. There was something about her which was optimistic, as a survivor. As a woman during that time, parts of her were more adaptable towards things around her.

 

SHERYL: So it’s about looking at a female perspective, which was silenced by these narratives that have reduced her to a very stereotypical tragic figure.

ELSA: Yeah, a very tragic figure. Sometimes, when you’re very connected to your creative work, you want to be at the centre of it and push it forward. But she did all of that within a few years and then decided to take a step back. She didn’t want to be in interviews or push her work anymore. I felt like she was very passionate about what she was writing, but maybe she had nothing else to write about anymore.

 

NATALIE: What about Wan stood out the most to you, or were there other unexpected things you found interesting during your research? 

ELSA: I think it was still the fact that she disappeared. That was very intriguing. I was thinking, would I ever want to disappear? Even if people offered me work—directing or writing scripts—would I still step back? 

In my script, I imagined that she might have spent her later years in her garden, maybe teaching students, or doing other things in her life. Even during the Occupation in Singapore, she was resourceful—she opened her own coffee shop for business. I felt that part of her would have definitely carried on after her disappearance, doing things connected to her stories, but also reflecting her personality outside of filmmaking.

 

NATALIE: Yeah, that’s also interesting—the role of creative labour. Is that something you’ve been thinking about too?

ELSA:  Yeah. Filmmaking really forces you to be present—you have to talk about it and be there so someone knows who’s behind the film. For a film to be historically recorded or archived, your name needs to be there, somewhere. With projects that we’ve worked on, we want to be credited really badly. But it’s almost like she decided that she doesn’t care about it. This made me think about how important archiving is. 

 

NATALIE: It’s almost like Wan Hoi-Ling resisted being archived.

ELSA: Yeah, maybe because so much of her was archived before. She realised, and decided, “No, I want to write my own story.”

 

NATALIE: I was also curious about your practice, obsessions, and interests in the past few years, and how this commission connects to your practice. You’ve done a lot—fashion, set design, film in a traditional sense, even programming, curating.

ELSA: I would say over the years, I’ve realised my work is always very emotionally driven. Regardless of whether I write the story first or plan scenarios, I always think about the colours, textures, and the emotions. Even for this film, I imagined Wan Hoi-Ling in every scene, what she would feel, which parts of her body would be in the frame—her back, her hands, hyper close-up moments. I do think my background in fashion influenced this, making me very attentive to details. Whenever I plan a photo or film, there are always a lot of details I fixate on within the frame.

I also made another similar film with miniatures, but that one had people and scenes inside. But this one is mostly purely object-based, with close-ups on colours. Over the last two or three years, I’ve really gotten into prop-making and set designing, so I fixated on making everything very still. Adding to the fact that it’s all from my imagination, I translated what’s in my mind into a tangible version—a 3D version of it.

 

NATALIE: Maybe we can talk a bit about objects, then. Since you’ve been involved in prop design, which particular objects were you drawn to, or what kinds of props were you referencing?

ELSA:  I would say in general, if I’m not making the props myself, I like found objects—it could be a brush, a small glass container—things that have been used by someone else. I feel like there’s already a strong personality in these objects that I can attach to the film I’m making. Even if I don’t know the purpose at first, I eventually find a symbolic meaning for it.

Sometimes, when I envision a prop or do set design, I don’t immediately understand why the image came to mind. Only after making it do I see why—it makes sense in the colours and textures. But during the process, it’s almost tunnel vision. I’m completely focused on the object and its role in the scene. I get very fixated, and I just have to see it through to the end and do it.

These are the shoes I used to represent Wan Hoi-Ling. It’s a very simple pair of shoes, but when I saw it at the thrift store, it struck me. It’s classic, something someone would wear in the 1930s, but at the same time, there’s something very blank about it. I can imagine the person wearing it, but it also leaves room for other imagination, because it’s white.

 

NATALIE: It’s almost like a screen that you can project onto.

ELSA: Exactly. I wanted everything to feel staged, emphasising the idea that these aren’t real events but my own projection of what I think she felt.

NATALIE: You’ve been in New York for the last three years now. Would you like to share about the evolution of your practice?

ELSA: Working between Singapore and New York, I almost wish I was in Singapore making the film. Making it here [in New York] felt different. Even if I wanted to do outdoor scenes, there was almost no way—the landscape and the visual inspiration from the environment here were very different, which is why I said it felt quite lonely making it. If I had been at home, I think I would have come up with the same story, but it might have felt different making it. Here, I was mostly working inside my home. I thought maybe I could shoot outdoors, and one day I went around a park I really like, but it just looked so different. Even if I tried to fake it, the feeling wasn’t there.

Even Chinatown here would look too different. It has become a big melting pot—a mesh of different parts of Chinese culture coming together. Also, it’s very recognisable, because so many people shoot in Manhattan’s Chinatown. If someone looked at it, they’d immediately know it was New York.

 

NATALIE: In Juliet’s Dinner, you used a similar language of dioramas, but it was a music video. You had an actor, a human figure, and in your fashion work you also shoot a lot of people. But with this work, there aren’t any people. Is that something you like, shooting more props, or is it quite different?

ELSA: I still like shooting half-and-half—with props and with people interacting with them. But for this project, I kept contemplating whether I wanted to shoot an actual sequence with people. At the same time, I felt I couldn’t do Wan Hoi-Ling justice if I shot a person. That’s why it had to be purely imagined. If I wanted it to exist in the space of imagination, I needed to fully commit to building a model of her within the miniatures and finding different objects.

It was also a good challenge that made me dive into the relationship between object and emotion—how to create consistent visual clues throughout the scenes so the audience recognises that this object represents this person, and another object represents someone else.

NATALIE: Could you share more about these object–emotion connections?

ELSA: For example, the confetti was something I was really drawn to. I watched a film that had a party sequence filled with confetti in the air. There was a never-ending, celebratory feeling, but it also seemed fake, like an orchestrated moment. When I got the confetti, I saw that the reflective parts were very interesting to capture. So much of Wan Hoi-Ling’s filmmaking was about light—light burning into the film. I wanted to carry that into my work, letting those specks of light run continuously through the film. With confetti, sequins, and light projection. 

To represent them, I relied on photos because there’s no footage of Wan Hoi-Ling and Hou Yao. In her photo, I couldn’t see much beyond her face and the upper half of her body, so I had to imagine what she was wearing and what people wore at that time. Since her photos were in black and white, I imagined the colours and patterns. One interview described her as very brightly dressed and upbeat, so I put her in bright colours throughout.

 

NATALIE: Where was this interview from?

That interview came from an anti-Chinese article that included an excerpt from a Chinese newspaper called Yu Le (娱乐). I couldn’t find the original online, but the article had a section where they interviewed her and other filmmakers or artists during the Japanese Occupation about what they were doing and how they felt about the film industry. They described her as brightly dressed, upbeat, and teaching a student—even though she only had one.

  

NATALIE: You mentioned certain anecdotes, but was there anything unexpected you discovered in the process of creating the work?

ELSA: Even in her interviews, she seemed almost unfazed—not unfazed, but very unaffected—about what had happened to her. What shocked me was realising that Wan Hoi-Ling and Hou Yao went through the war in Singapore. They were invited to Singapore to make films, and then, eventually, almost by fate, what happened to them happened. I kept thinking, what if they hadn’t gone to Singapore? What if they had stayed in Hong Kong? Would it have been a very different story, a very different history, for her? But fate had it that they went to Singapore—he died, and that shaped her story. I wanted to highlight that in the script: toward the end, it’s less about the tragedy and more about her accepting that it was destined, something inevitable.

 

NATALIE: If you had to summarise your work in three words, what would they be

ELSA: “Emotional” is one of them. 

 

NATALIE: That emotive connection is what brings in the human element—even though we never see a human, the emotion is still human.

ELSA: Yes. I’d also say it’s “ghostly”. At times, when making the miniatures of her, I felt a certain presence, a certain pressure, because I was representing her in different ways. I kept asking myself, would she say this, would she do this? I couldn’t know for sure, but it had to feel close to the specific kinds of films she made.

I’m trying to think of a last word, maybe something for the still-life aspect, like the props.

 

NATALIE: I’m also thinking more about the technique, the dollhouse aspect—the craftiness of it. There’s a very tactile, handmade feel to the work. The sets look theatrical and playful.

ELSA: Yes, it ties back to the installation. I thought so much about the installation before even considering the visuals for the film, and in the end, the two had a really nice connection.

 

NATALIE: Yes, it’s very theatrical. The backdrop of the Great Wall theme park had lots of performances, so the way it’s set also feels that way.

ELSA: So maybe that’s the word: “theatrical”. Because so much of it is a staged and performed sequence.

When I was making the work, I felt this pressure to do her justice. Not that I saw or felt her ghost, but her image was ingrained in my mind—that one photo of her.

SHERYL: You felt the weight of representing her in a way that would be true to what she was?

NATALIE: Her spirit.

ELSA: Yeah, almost like her spirit. When I was thinking of a title for the work, I went through a few ideas. I considered “the ghost of her” but it didn’t feel right. Eventually, I chose the word “secret,” because so much of what I imagined felt like her secret life, behind her films, that nobody knew about.

 

SHERYL: The person behind the public persona.

NATALIE: What do you hope audiences will gain from your work?

ELSA: I hope they learn about her. Not a lot of people do. When friends ask me about the project and I tell them about this filmmaker, everyone is intrigued by her story—especially the fact that she disappeared. I think audiences can gather that even though we know so much about her through her filmography, there’s also a real side of her that we’ll never be able to get to.

We can only imagine those periods of time and how others around her felt, which might have informed how she felt. As a woman in the 1930s, it was definitely difficult. Then, the war was difficult. 1960s Hong Kong would have been very different too. I even asked my grandparents about it, since they lived through that time, and they gave me insight into how they felt—you just had to keep going, be very adaptable. Maybe that was how she felt too.

  

NATALIE: I find the use of found objects very interesting because you’re assembling all these random things to call to mind the memory of a person we don’t really know much about. And with the objects, you also don’t know who used to own them.

ELSA: Exactly. It’s a lot of lost-and-found. The sculptures in the sketches are very abstract, but for the final version, I was deciding whether to create something entirely new or use the found objects. I think I’ll bring the found objects back, either displaying them directly or integrating them into a sculpture within the installation.

  

NATALIE: Reflecting on your practice, this work has a strong emotional element, which recurs in your work, but also introduces new aspects, like the use of objects, sets without people, found footage, and celluloid. The “lost-and-found” theme appears both in a material and textural form, which feels fresh. The artists in this project have interpreted the idea of lost film in very different ways. Because of your background in set design and fashion, it comes across in a very tactile, textural way, which is really nice to see.

ELSA: The film part is interesting because when both of us tried to look for more of her films, it was really difficult to find anything that wasn’t with Hou Yao. So having the physical reel for her felt almost like something being found.

I have another roll of film I want to use for the found footage—burn it onto the film and see what that would look like. I did one experiment where I played a moving image on my computer screen and filmed it using the Bolex camera. I’m interested to see how that translates on film—what it captures and how it looks.

 

NATALIE: I was just thinking about the textural and tactile quality of Hou Yao’s silent film, A Poet from the Sea (1927).

ELSA: And also the colours. It had a lot of double exposures. That’s something special about the Bolex—you can rewind in-camera and shoot over it, then go back again. I tried that a couple of times, so we’ll see what comes out. It’s always tricky. The sound of the Bolex is also very specific. While shooting alone and hearing the film constantly, I imagined how they would have worked at that time. It felt as if I had staged myself in the same scenario—winding the film, shooting it, listening only to the sound of the film reel running.

 

NATALIE: Are you constructing a soundtrack for the film? What are your current thoughts on that?

ELSA: There is a voiceover. I have a friend from Singapore with a very nice, contemplative voice, and I want her to voice Wan Hoi-Ling. Her name is Karen. She’s not in the film industry, but she’s someone I met here. She’s Southern Chinese, and her family moved to Singapore from China around that time. Talking to her felt like a nice connection to have.

The script is in English because my Chinese isn’t great. I considered translating it to Chinese, but I realised there might be a disconnect if someone else translated it. So, we decided that on the day of recording, we’d workshop some parts in Mandarin and some in Hokkien. I’m trying to reflect what they might have spoken at the time—Cantonese, Mandarin, or Hokkien, representing the spirit of overseas Chinese.

Karen speaks a little Hokkien, which is perfect. We’ll keep some lines in English, since some parts come from my imagination. The three languages can create a kind of disconnection and connection between what is real and what is imagined.

I came to this conclusion about three different languages or voices because I was talking with a friend who had to translate scripts recently. They had watched a film titled Việt and Nam (dir. Trương Minh Quý, 2024), and we were talking about how language is fluid—because of translation, subtitles, and the original language, there’s always an added layer. It’s never one-to-one, which is how I felt while watching Spirit of the Overseas Chinese.

I had to watch Wan Hoi-Ling’s film with my grandfather because I couldn’t catch everything. The film had no subtitles. I understood some of it, but sometimes the delivery of emotions in Hokkien felt inaccurate—they could say something happy, but the delivery was fierce. My grandfather helped interpret. He explained that the story is very sad, about the hardships of people who migrated to Singapore from China, and that it was true to his time. It was interesting to watch with someone who understood the language more. He was like a translator for me.

 

NATALIE: That’s amazing. When you say language is fluid, I feel that’s relevant to the work. I read somewhere that Wan Hoi-Ling was often thought to be a man. There’s a certain gender fluidity to it. As a woman making films in a male-dominated industry back then, it would have been very different.

ELSA: I wrote it into the script—she knew that to be a part of the film industry, she needed to work with a man. That man became her partner. She was very driven; she knew she needed to be mentored by an established man because historical records centred on him. Her name appears too, but there’s more information about him. It’s my imagination, but I think a part of her knew that that might be what she had to do.

Natalie: I’m really excited to see the work come together. Thank you so much for today.

 

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

In this interview, artist Elsa Wong reflects on how she transposed her research into the film’s three-part narrative, working with a variety of […]

content.rendered:
In his essay, “The Road People”, poet Gwee Li Sui argues that the road may be the most appropriate metaphor for the Singaporean condition:

“The road—more than the skyscraper or the economy—is the quintessential image of urban processes. The road is not just the city’s life-giver and shaper, its circulatory system, but also a paradoxically unliveable space, a desert stretch.”¹

Singapore is a restless nation that has embraced speed, efficiency, and progress as its core values. Despite the scarcity of land, a significant proportion of our land surface is given over to motorways, with new roads paved every year, privileging the use of automobiles over other forms of transportation. Representing affluence, convenience and air-conditioned comfort, a car is a status symbol in this country, a sign of having made it. The bitter irony, of course, is that there is no destination. We are perpetually on the move, striving towards a horizon we can never reach.

Refuge Island, a programme of short films from Singapore, takes mobility as its theme, exploring how ceaseless movement came to be a prerequisite for survival and social advancement, and where one might seek respite from the merciless demands of the road. The programme title proposes an answer to the latter question, with recourse to a commonplace architectural feature: the refuge island, a section of pavement built in the middle of busy streets that lack marked crosswalks or traffic lights. The elevated concrete block provides pedestrians with a safe place to pause and survey the situation, to wait for the traffic to ebb.

 

Firing the Ignition

Refuge Island opens with Nelson Yeo’s Myths (2016), which follows two children as they discover a vintage headset and watch an old film reel in an abandoned lot. This simple plot belies a more complex question, of how our historical legacy of itinerancy bears on a younger generation of urbanites.

Myths nods to our roots and rootlessness, with reference to two earlier works from Singapore. The first is Edwin Thumboo’s Ulysses by the Merlion, playing through the salvaged headset. Written from the perspective of the mythic hero, Ulysses, this iconic poem imagines him encountering the Merlion, a strange hybrid of fish and lion. To the worldly-wise adventurer, the chimeric mascot embodies Singapore’s incoherent identity, a crude synthesis of ancestral cultures and modern influences.

The second intertextual reference is Tunang Pak Dukun (1960), a Cathay-Keris production from the golden years of studio film in Singapore. In this film within a film, a musical number shows villagers returning to their kampong while singing Pulang Merantau, in anticipation of their homecoming. Invoking the practice of merantau, a centuries-old ritual of migration and a rite of passage common throughout the Malay Archipelago, Myths posits a historical continuity from the nomadic patterns of the past to our globalised present.²

 

 

Starting with this film frames the programme around the figure of the sojourner: the Homeric hero; the wanderer of the Nusantara; the curious children transported to a bygone era. The title, Myths, reminds us that there are dominant narratives we have subscribed to, or spun for ourselves, as an immigrant society negotiating the tension between perambulation and staying put, change and constancy.

While Yeo offers a slightly romanticised, nostalgic vision of wandering, Berita Singapura: Road Safety Measures (1967) plunges us into the rhythms of post-independence Singapore, where mobility is strictly regulated. The state-produced commercial is one in a series of multilingual newsreels that aired weekly during the first decade of television in Singapore, and the heavy-handed messaging illustrates the making of a road people.

We see examples of deviant behaviour like jaywalking, speeding and reckless driving, as well as the wreckage of cars, with shattered glass and crumpled metal visualising the tragic consequences of flouting traffic rules. A commentator recites statistics about the thousands of deaths caused by road accidents each year. Hyper-vigilance is encouraged, and the individual is advised to take responsibility for themselves, to manage the risks of the road. 

 

 

Against the backdrop of a rapidly modernising city, the unruly masses need coordination and containment. The physical topography moulds its citizens’ psychic landscape, as urban space is coded into zones of relative safety, with pedestrians keeping to designated pavements and overhead bridges. Citizens are schooled in road etiquette, through the iconography of stop signs, speed limits, and traffic lights. The road is not just a metaphor, but a mechanism for mass conditioning,

Decades of didactic control predictably produce a pliant, if dispassionate, population. Carol Ho and Teo Mei-Ann’s Not Here (2008) sets us in contemporary Singapore, where white-collar workers eke out their living in an environment geared toward profit and productivity. Two professionals take in the panoramic view from their office, but it offers no visual delight, only the sight of cranes, roads and buildings stretching as far as the eye can see. Confronted by this dull prospect, they start to feel the faint stirrings of lust.

 

 

But their attempts to find a spot to consummate their tentative desires are thwarted at every turn. An office bathroom, the backseat of a car, a HDB stairwell, and even a hotel room, prove inadequate. Each space is either too public, too cramped, or too trite—even when they can secure a space for themselves, they hear another couple in the next room, and suddenly feel like a stereotype, engaging in an illicit workplace affair. In these urban settings, the two are self-conscious, their bodies bumping awkwardly against each other. Human connection is strained, and verbal communication is muted. There is little dialogue, except for a single refrain, “not here”, muttered each time the characters fail to find a satisfactory place for sex. The city is no place for erotic pleasure. 

Only when they go off road and enter a forest clearing do they discover a sense of privacy, a reprieve from scrutiny and surveillance. The lush beauty and sensuality of nature, with the gentle hum of insects, offers a peaceful, secluded site for intimacy. As their inhibitions and internalised shame fall away, the man whispers, “here”. The camera, trained intently on the characters throughout the film, finally pulls away, leaving the pair to their lovemaking. 

 

 

These characters do not fully transcend the trope of the Singaporean professional desperate to escape the tedium of corporate culture. The retreat to nature and the release of sex might displace our energies or distract us from the monotony of work but cannot free us from the demands of capitalism. Other liberatory possibilities are intimated, in the freedom of motion. As they coast down the streets on a motorcycle, the camera lingers on the woman’s hands clutching his waist, his own fingers wrapped around the handlebars. These moments conjure the thrill of the ride, recalling similar scenes in Eating Air (Kelvin Tong and Jasmine Ng, 1999) and Fallen Angels (Wong Kar Wai, 1995), where lovers seek automotive exhilaration as an antidote to urban alienation. The rush of the open road is fleeting, but enough to make them feel alive. 

 

Accelerating

What does movement mean to us, and how are its meanings mobilised in service of different agendas? In Berita Singapura: Nation on the Move (1965), movement is synonymous with survival and success. The newsreel shows the cityscape taking shape, as Singapore is terraformed and sculpted into a model of efficient urban living. Construction proceeds apace, with plans for more public flats and university buildings to house and educate the population. Nicoll Highway is widened to relieve traffic congestion, and Jurong Oil Refinery is projected to boost our economy. Even our landmass poses no limit, with reclamation works underway to extend our terrestrial boundaries. From the earliest days of independence, an ideology of pragmatism is cemented in our infrastructure.

 

 

In a self-congratulatory voiceover, the commentator extolls the nation’s aspirations for progress and the collective commitment to securing our future. With the benefit of retrospect, we might temper the heady optimism of the developmental state. We know that the pursuit of incessant growth does not lead only to gains; over time, social and environmental deficits accrue.

A particularly ironic effect of Singapore’s streamlined transport networks is the need for dedicated physical activity, with a concomitant demand for expensive fitness classes and gym memberships. Tan Pin Pin’s documentary walk walk (2023) considers the humbler act of walking, and the range of reflections it inspires.

 

 

Through her interviews, Tan chronicles their motivations for taking walks. For a group of middle-aged women, their social walking club is a source of mutual support. For a visual practitioner, traversing the city by foot is a more solitary recreation, a way to find mental clarity and to notice the peculiarities of her neighbourhood. For artist Amanda Heng, walking is a gesture of resistance. Her public performances, Walking the Stool (1999–) and Let’s Walk (1997–) turn the streets into a stage, challenging social norms and protesting regressive societal attitudes of women.

All the interviewees are women, and a common thread across their responses is the urge to carve out space for themselves. Movement takes on a distinct valence—it is not the interminable march forward, but an intentional mode of being present, cultivating appreciation for the world around us, and exercising bodily autonomy. At one point, Tan asks, “Where are you going?” and Heng replies, “Going for a walk.” This exchange upsets the teleological assumption that we walk to go places. We walk for the joy of it, a sentiment captured in the charming phrase, “walk walk”. Alluding to local expressions like kia kia (Teochew) or jalan-jalan (Malay), it connotes a leisurely stroll.

 

 

In contrast, Berita Singapura: Keeping Fit (1967) traffics in the overtly moralistic discourse of healthy living. The newsreel features bodybuilding, martial arts, and military drills as examples of the training regimes people should adopt to keep fit. Bodies are instrumentalised and those who fail to bulk up or slim down are “going to be left behind”, the commentator warns, conflating physical movement with social mobility. This bleak vision of physical training has more to do with discipline and conformity than the personal journey, inducting us into the cult of self-optimisation.

 

Idling  

The rules of the road may already be written, but navigating those rules creatively can be a practice of self-expression within an oppressive environment. Ryan Benjamin Lee’s experimental animation, Axis (2022) takes inspiration from late artist Chng Seok Tin, in particular, her drypoint prints, Social Climbers (1992) and Gold Rush (1993), which depict human figures locked in a brutal, unforgiving race for wealth and status; and Game of Chess (1999–2001), an installation that depicts life as a series of calculated, strategic moves.³

 

 

Borrowing from Chng’s monochromatic palette, Axis starts with a series of black and white rectangular shapes in gridded patterns. These motifs could indicate either traffic junctions and crossings, if we are looking from above, at an aerial view of the city; or high-rise buildings, if we are looking up from below, at street level. The horizontal and vertical planes converge and come apart, as the axis of vision tilts and the film plays with perspective.

Colour seeps into the world with the introduction of a human-like figure. The monochrome structures mutate, morphing from a chessboard into a synth pad on which the figure frolics. Piano keys sound as it hops from square to square, releasing tendrils of vibrant colour as it interacts with the grid. However rigid the existing structures, it is possible to discover whimsy and dance within the lines.

Gladys Ng’s Every Floor Looks the Same (2022) is more circumspect about the potential for originality, in a country where passion is routinely stifled. The synopsis tells us that Osmanthüs is languishing—a term popularised by pandemic lockdowns, denoting a state of joyless, aimless stagnation. Osmanthüs certainly fits the description. As she lazes at the playground, attends music lessons, and takes the bus, she remains detached from everything. She quietly observes the city, but the homogenous cityscape rouses little excitement in our young protagonist. 

 

Around her, empty husks of buildings mirror the hollowness of life. The drone of construction, tree pruning and estate maintenance never lets up, constituting the musical signature of a city and its discontents. This incessant mechanical soundscape is jarringly interrupted by a child’s protracted scream at an amusement park. Whether out of terror or glee, it is a rare display of emotion. Another is a hand drawn poster for a missing bird. Amidst flyers advertising PSLE tuition and grassroots events, the childish sketch and heartfelt appeal stands out. The missing pet eventually finds its way back, in the form of a stuffed toy that Osmanthüs tapes to the noticeboard. But the actual bird is never found, nor even glimpsed.

The film might seem to end on a cynical note, confirming an inauthentic and soulless existence, if all we are left with is a semblance of the real. But I imagine that the living bird has embarked on its own merantau, departing on a line of flight and perhaps finding a home in the wilderness. And there may indeed be a way out, as recurring motifs of alluring greenery and open sky, framed through stairwells and windows, suggest openings to an elsewhere.

In Transit

Refuge Island alternates between archival material and contemporary short films, generating antithesis between independent media and state propaganda, and an anachronistic whiplash that subverts the linear logic of the road. This sequencing stages the dynamic contest of ideas that characterises the conceptual economy of the short film in Singapore.

A medium of brevity, the short film is eminently portable.⁴ Like TikTok reels that feed off our cooked attention spans, state commercials slip into the cracks between regular programming, reaching a broad viewership. But the short film is as much a tool of corporate and government control as a means of personal expression and artistic experimentation, of charting alternative perspectives. Independent shorts function as refuge islands, too. Often anthologised, they form archipelagic configurations with other films. The short moving image works included in this programme find affinities with multiple forms of arts, including poetry, printmaking, and performance. Migrating across galleries, cinemas, and bus interchanges, and circulating online, they are irrepressibly mobile.

Paradoxically, an actual refuge island is a space of paralysis, offering momentary respite but not meaningful rest. Perched on a median, stranded between an onslaught of cars from both directions, I usually feel tense, exposed and vulnerable. There is clearly no exit from the punitive expressway that is Singapore. Rather, the safety island is designed and sanctioned for pedestrian use, so whatever refuge can be sought exists on the terms of the central urban planner, part of an architecture of control. Yet, that sliver of concrete, just wide enough to accommodate an individual, affords some breathing room amidst the relentless traffic—a refuge from the road that is precarious, and precious, nonetheless.

 

 

Footnotes

  1. Gwee, Li Sui. “The Road People: Poetry and Urban (Im)Mobility in Singapore.” Asiatic, vol. 2, no. 2, 2008, pp. 134-149.
  2. Mohd Erman Maharam. “Transnational cultures of Malaysian, Indonesian, Singaporean, and Philippine national cinema.” Transnational Screens, vol. 12, no, 2, pp. 134-149.
  3. Cheng, Jia Yun. Chng Seok Tin: Drawn through a Press. National Gallery Singapore. 2021.
  4. Harvey, Sophia Siddique. “Nomadic trajectories: Mapping short film production in Singapore.” Inter-Asia Cultural Studies, vol. 8, no.2, 2007, pp. 262-276.

 

About the Writer

Tracey Toh is an arts writer and researcher who practises creative criticism in response to film, literature and performance.

content.rendered:
Unassuming yet packed with the vibrancy of youth, director Nobuhiro Yamashita’s Linda Linda Linda (2005) is celebrating its twentieth anniversary this year with a new remaster in 4K. Starring Korean actress Doona Bae (Broker, The Host, Take Care of My Cat), the film follows a high school girl band who loses their main vocalist due to a falling out. Scrambling to pull together a performance for their high school’s annual bunkasai (school cultural festival), they hastily recruit Korean exchange student Son (Bae) as their new vocalist. 

 

With few dramatic twists and turns, Linda Linda Linda has been described as ‘mellow’ and ‘reserved’, setting it apart from a dearth of more explosive Japanese high school and coming of age films. Its roots lie more in the Japanese slice of life genre, focusing on the mundane everyday and purity of the moment. Perhaps, this is why it has remained such a cult hit, with audiences outside Japan who relate to the universal charm of playing music for the pure love of it, and gaining a new generation of audience twenty years on. 

Following sold out sessions at the Asian Film Archive and an announcement of encore screenings later in the year, AFA’s Natalie Ng got to chat with director Nobuhiro Yamashita to reflect on Linda Linda Linda’s enduring popularity twenty years on. 

 

Congratulations on an amazing 2024 with multiple films released including Karaoke Iko! and Ghost Cat Anzu, and now in 2025 with Linda Linda Linda celebrating its 20th anniversary. How does it feel talking about two films you made recently and then reflecting 20 years ago when you made Linda Linda Linda?

With Linda Linda Linda celebrating its 20th anniversary and remastered, I’ve definitely been reflecting about being a director for the last twenty-five years. It’s been an interesting turning point in my career, talking about all my past films in the last few years. 

 

 

Linda Linda Linda, Lalala at Rock Bottom and Karaoke Iko! have a focus on music. Are you particularly drawn to films with music as a subject, and did making Linda Linda Linda influence you with making the other two films? 

I do think it’s exactly that. I think after working on Linda Linda Linda, films like Lalala at Rock Bottom and Karaoke Iko! fell into my lap. It’s not like I have a background in music or I’m a musician or extremely passionate about music, but I think that after Linda Linda Linda it was thought that oh, he’s a director who can handle the stories revolving around music. I respect and love music but I wouldn’t consider myself a director specialising in music.

 

I read that producer Hiroyuki Negishi brought the script to you. What made you interested in making Linda Linda Linda? Was it the characters or story or something else?

When producer Negishi brought the script to me, the original script was about an all-girl band doing a cover of The Blue Hearts. But it was more about them participating in a contest, and it was about a success story as a band. I was not very into this storyline, but producer Negishi gave me the opportunity to develop this story together, and that’s how I got into it.

 

I also read in that same interview that the original script for Linda Linda Linda was more purely entertainment, but you eventually made quite a lot of changes to it. Can you talk about what are some of the changes you made from the script to the final film?

The biggest change was about using music to become a success story. I didn’t think music should have an element of ‘winning’ and ‘losing’. I really wanted just the purity of performing music. So that’s why instead of a contest, I changed it to a school festival performance. Originally between the characters, there was a lot of drama. There were love stories and love triangles and such. It was a lot more splashy, with all the drama, so I completely changed that in the story to just being about girls being friends and staying up late to practice for a performance. 

 

 

The simple story of just being with friends and playing music is also why I think the film is so well-loved. But I would like to ask for your thoughts on why you think that 20 years later, Linda Linda Linda has remained so beloved? Today, there are adults revisiting the film, but also many young people who were not even born when the movie first came out in 2005 discovering it for the first time.

I really think it’s because I didn’t add anything splashy to the story. All the dramatic pizzaz moments, I took it out from the original script, and it is really a film that focuses on what being a teenager is really like. It’s about teenage life, and the purity of those moments of youth that the audience will be able to relate to. If it had all those dramatics, it would be a different story with a completely different feeling to what the film eventually turned out to be. 

 

I saw that all the cast members reunited for the 20th anniversary screening in Japan, and Kenichi Matsuyama and Bae Doona even recreated the confession scene in the film—how was it like meeting and talking to your cast 20 years later?

It was like a real reunion. After we made Linda Linda Linda, everyone went their separate ways, we didn’t have a lot of contact with one another. Looking at everyone twenty years later, everyone has grown up very elegantly, and I really felt like a school teacher, going back to a school reunion and seeing my students all grown up. 

 

 

How did you come to cast Bae Doona in the film? Twenty years on, she is now an international star who has worked all over the world. What was it like for her as the only Korean person in an all-Japanese film production? 

I think not knowing Japanese and coming into a Japanese film production, it was probably pretty stressful for [Bae Doona]. But even then, she was very mindful as a professional actress. If I gave her any notes, she would listen well and think about it carefully. She was very strict with herself, so now that I see her being active all over the world, and even in Hollywood, it is really easy to understand why she would be able to accomplish that. She was a very strong person. 

And the reason why we came to offer her a role in this film was purely because I was a fan of hers.

 

Which films did you see her in that you became a fan of hers?

I’m not very sure about the English title—I think it is called Barking Dogs Don’t Bite? I saw her in that movie and fell in love with her.

 

 

In Singapore, the screenings of Linda Linda Linda have all sold out which we are very excited about! We gave out guitar picks designed by our local distributor, Anticipate Pictures and invited a music shop to do a pop up at our theatre. Can you say a few words for the audiences in Singapore?

This film I made twenty years ago—I was young back then, the cast was young back then, and even the crew! But I really felt like it depicts everyone’s youth from the cast and crew to myself. I’m really happy that everyone will be able to see it again, or see it for the first time. But also as a film that’s about music, I feel that it shows the power of music, and how it goes out to the world and transcends language and countries. It is able to touch everybody. And then that leads into the power of film, and what the power of film can do. I really think this film is best watched on a big screen with an audience, and if everyone could watch it on a big screen, that would be wonderful.

 

 

Do you have any interesting memories of shooting Linda Linda Linda and do you have a favourite scene from the film? 

I was so young back then! I was so anxious and nervous filming then that I don’t remember much during the filming process. There’s a dialogue in the film that goes something like how you don’t often really remember when you’re in the moment, because you’re just so into it. But I do remember after shooting, when I returned back to Tokyo, I felt really lonely. I went back home, and I thought to myself, “Oh, I’m all alone.” I think it’s because during the production, being with everyone, from the cast to the crew, it was all so fun. 

 

 

About the favourite scene—you know how there’s a scene at night, where the girls are in their club room and they are practicing performing “My Right Hand”. The camera is on the outside taking the shot of them just practicing. I really love that shot and that scene because the girls look like they’re in their own world, in their own time, in the moment. And you as the audience, you’re sort of peeking in to watch them. That is really my favourite scene. 

 

You’ve said before that you love trying new things and genres—are you working on anything that you can talk about, or what kind of film would you like to make in the future?

I’m working on two films right now, and they’re both based on manga, and they’re both about youth. Hopefully we can start shooting next year. I’m in my fifties now, so in the future, I would really love to work on something that reflects my generation. 

 

Many thanks to Satsuki Yamashita for interpreting this interview.

content.rendered:
As 2024 comes to an end, this issue of the Asian Cinema Digest highlights available screenings for the holiday season, as well as best-of lists, opinion pieces and reflective interviews to sum up our cinema journey this year.

TO SEE

Asian Film Archive: Edward Yang’s Four Favourite Films

Following up from a full retrospective of Edward Yang’s iconic oeuvre, the Asian Film Archive (AFA) presents 4 of the auteur’s favourite classic films: Nostalghia (1983) by Andrei Tarkovsky), My American Uncle (1980) by Alain Resnais, Blue Velvet (1986) by David Lynch and Aguirre, the Wrath of God (1972) by Werner Herzog, each having influenced Yang’s attitudes and approaches to his own practice.

The accompanying exhibition titled Retrospective: Edward Yang will also remain up at the atrium right outside the Oldham Theatre until 29 December 2024, allowing audiences a look at original props, artefacts, rare behind the scenes footage and more.

 

Asian Film Archive: 5 Christmas themed Singaporean films from the collection

The Asian Film Archive (AFA) holds and preserves a crucial repository of Singaporean and Southeast Asian films, some of which are available for viewing in the National Library of Singapore. Here are 5 Singaporean films set during or around the festive period that can be found on the shelf at the Lee Kong Chian Reference Library.

A Christmas Wish (2008) by Winston Chee

Notes written by an unseen hand magically manifest to help bridge the communication gap between a young girl and her busy parents so that her wish for both of them to spend Christmas with her this year is fulfilled.

All I Want for Christmas (2006) by Chang Yee Yeo

A woman has a film production career so demanding that she is left with little time for her novelist partner, even on holidays and special occasions. He tries to be patient and she in turn tries her utmost to cope with work and the marriage, but they soon meet with disappointments that could just scar their relationship irrevocably.

All My Presents (2002) by Wee Li Lin

Sue holds a Christmas party and excitedly prepares specially bought presents for all her guests. The lack of appreciation from some of her guests though, leads to much disappointment.

The Christmas Boy (2009) by Henry Wong

A young boy tries to befriend his elderly and unhappy neighbour. With the help of his friends, the boy brings love and warmth into the old man’s life by reconciling him with his son and inviting him to a Christmas party.

The Carrot Cake Conversations (2010) by Charmaine Teo, Michael Wang

Four strangers find themselves stranded in Singapore two days before Christmas. This is a story of how they find companionship over a plate of carrot cake and a conversation.

 

 

50th Metro Manila Film Festival

From 25 December 2024 to 7 January 2025, the 50th Metro Manila Film Festival presents 10 Filipino features and student short films in competition, vibrant works of varying genres and styles. Audiences can look forward to Pepe Diokno’s Isang Himala (2024), a screen adaptation of the stage musical based on Ishmael Bernal’s Himala (1982). The cautionary tale, which had also premiered in 1982 at the same festival to wide acclaim, tells the spiralling tale of Elsa, a young provincial girl who claims to have been visited by the Virgin Mary and begins exhibiting miracles.A restored Himala was previously screened at the Asian Film Archive as part of the special programme DIVINE, exploring filmic connections between femininity and the gendered notion of venerated goddesshood.

 

e-flux: Queer Strategies and Tentacles

Films and videos unpacking and subverting the intertwined concerns of queer liberation, survival, gentrification and resistance are streaming on e-flux’s screening room for free until March 2025. Curated by Rosa Barotsi and Zairong Xiang, Queer Strategies and Tentacles runs in 8 themed chapters, each running for 2 weeks. The current lineup, a double bill of 2 Chinese short films pondering a homoerotic gaze, features Shen Xin’s The Gray Critic (2015) and Peng Zuqiang’s Sight Leak (2022).

 

TO READ

MUBI Notebook: The Best Movie Posters of 2024

MUBI’s resident movie poster columnist Adrian Curry rounds up his top 10 movie posters of 2024, with A Traveller’s Needs (2024) coming out on top. Curry praises designer Brian Hung’s playful details that reflect the wry character of the film and its protagonist, played by Isabelle Huppert: the lush green of the neighbourhood park, twinkling lights in the far corner (which is actually the billing block), stone inscriptions of the film’s synopsis, a bottle of the character’s beloved makgeolli nestled in the grass. He also notes the poster’s resemblance to The Park, a 1910 painting by Gustav Klimt, in which green fern-like textures similarly take over most of the composition.

A Traveller’s Needs was previously screened at the Asian Film Archive as part of the special programme Rest & Relax, surrounding the contradictory bind of films exuding aesthetics of leisure and escapism while depicting underlying anxieties of our daily life.

The list also mentions Between Goodbyes (2024) by Jota Mun, sensitively composed with a torn silhouette from a photograph to underscore the film’s narrative of a Korean adoptee reconnecting with her birth family, and April (2024) by Déa Kulumbegashvili, a collage of overlaid textures: a wrinkled hospital sheet over backdrop of clouded blue skies, masking a large smear of blood. The film follows an ob-gyn moonlighting as an abortionist in rural Georgia.

 

Deadline: Navigating The Oscar Race: South Asian Cinema’s Quiet Surge As Shortlist Voting Begins

The end of the year also heralds the arrival of Oscar predictions, speculations and ‘For Your Consideration’ campaigns. Sunil Sadarangani highlights the surge of South Asian films that may contend for nominations besides India’s official entry, Lost Ladies (2023) by Kiran Rao: short films Anuja (2024) by Adam J. Graves and Me, Raani (2024) by Shivani Mehra, and features All We Imagine As Light (2024) by Payal Kapadia and The Glassworker (2024) by Usman Riaz. She comments positively on the critical and media attention these titles have gotten across the year, some bolstered by international film festivals, others by streaming platforms that have given the films an instant, wider reach.

 

IFFR Blog: Work with people you like: Aiko Masubuchi on Happyend

Fresh out of its world premiere at Venice’s Orizzonti section, Neo Sora’s fiction feature debut Happyend (2024) on surveillance and authoritarianism has travelled to many other prestigious festivals in Toronto, Busan, Singapore, with more premieres to come. Programmer, translator and producer Aiko Masubuchi reflects on her 7 year journey with Sora to make the film, the struggle of navigating fund applications, searching for affinities to build a team and finding her own way. She credits the Rotterdam Lab and the producers she met there in giving her the advice to “work with people you like”.

 

Rappler: ‘Vox Humana’: Director Don Eblahan brings the Cordilleras to Toronto film fest

Lé Baltar chats with filmmaker and musician Don Josephus Raphael Eblahan about his newest hybrid sci-fi/western short film Vox Humana (2024), about a transcendent encounter between a zoologist and a feral man she has been hired to attempt communication with. Don Eblahan’s narratives surround the cerebral, emotional and physical plights of indigenous people existing in post-colonial spaces and lands. In line with drawing out connections to the landscape, its textures and sounds, Vox Humana’s visuals are ruled by the majestic cordilleras and its natural light, while sound design was meticulously developed, namely through a fictional language of sounds and symbols used in the film. Don Eblahan is also developing a “feature film cousin” to Vox Humana, titled Hum, which tells a different story but retains similar genre experimentations.

 

TO SUBMIT

Call for Submissions: 49th Hong Kong International Film Festival

The Hong Kong International Film Festival is accepting submissions of features, shorts and documentaries that have not premiered in Hong Kong. The rules and regulations can be found here, and the deadline for submissions is 31 December 2024.

 

Call for Submissions: 3rd Mint Chinese Film Festival

Based in Keswick, UK, the Mint Chinese Film Festival programmes feature and short film competitions for films revolving around Chinese stories, communities, diaspora and cultural memories. They are accepting submissions of features above 60 minutes and shorts under 30 minutes produced between 2023 and 2024. The rules and regulations can be found here, and the deadline for submissions is 30 January 2025.

 

Call for Submissions: 18th Asian Film Awards

The annual Asian Film Awards is accepting submissions of Asian features above 60 minutes that have been screened theatrically or distributed in Asia in 2024, or received national awards/international premieres. The rules and regulations can be found here, and the deadline for submissions is 31 December 2024.

 

Call for Submissions: JEONJU Cinema Project – Next Edition (Film Fund)

The JEONJU Cinema Project aims to discover and support independent productions, and is accepting both Korean and international project submissions. Selected project(s) will receive up to 50,000,000 KRW of funding. The rules and regulations can be found here, and the deadline for submissions is 20 December 2024. 

 

Call for Participation: IMDA Short-Form Content Grant

The Short-Form Content Grant is open for short films below 40 minutes by a Singapore Citizen or Permanent Resident director or producer. The project must not be a commissioned or school project. The rules and regulations can be found here, and the deadline for submissions is 7 January 2025.

 

This edition of the Asian Cinema Digest was compiled by Renee Ng. The Asian Cinema Digest is a monthly compilation of content taking place internationally involving Asian cinema and the moving image. Featured programmes are not representative of AFA’s views and are unaffiliated to the AFA unless otherwise stated.
